title: Why Mario Bauza left Cuba in 1930
summary: Mario, disillusioned when lesser white musicians took his jobs, left for New York as did Socarras, Lico Jimenez and Rico, as talking pictures ended jobs for black players.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I see. Okay. I get the picture now at the twenties. All right, let's go back to Agabama. How long did you remain with them?
From 1933 to 36.
Okay. In 1930, Mario Bauza left Cuba for New York City. What brought that about?
Discrimination.
Tell me about it.
He was disillusioned. There was disillusion to be such an accomplished musician and see second-rate and third-rater taking his place, so he was disgusted.
In other words, he lost jobs because he was an Afro-Cuban?
Yes
And they were giving it to white musicians who were less proficient than he was.
Absolutely. Not even half, a third.
Humm - I see.
The same happened with Socarras, the same happened with Lico Jimenez, the same happened with Rico, he was the top ten flute player in the world, and he left Cuba...
Because they were black they couldn't...
...he went to Paris, and I think he died in Paris. He left Cuba in 1930 or '29.
Okay. Socarras......
.... and Sotilla too.
......Socarras says that once the talk movie came, The Jazz Singer, they knew that jazz, eh, black musicians wouldn't get jobs there, they would hire whites. Is that true?
Whites, whites.
Okay. He came, Socarras came in twenty-eight, Mario came in 1930 - ah - Do you remember when he left Cuba?
Yes, definetely.
Tell me about that time.

Well, we were together always. The last year that he played in Cuba was at the Montmartre, with Gilberto Valdes. He made a combination because that was all-white band, but Gilberto Valdes was very liberal. Being white, he was very liberal and he hired Mario.
Mario told me that the last band he worked with and he was discriminated against, was -ah- Curbelo's father, Jose Curbelo's father.
Yeah.
Did he ever tell you about that?
Oh yeah, I know it like a book.
